title: Deterministic Output & Toolchain Latency Review
summary: Deep dive on latency overheads introduced by deterministic/JSON-constrained decode modes and function-call tooling. Agreed to run a focused microbenchmark across quantized variants with KV cache on/off and two batching configs; Redwood to deliver benchmark harness and draft config recommendations for Penumbra's streaming ingestion path. Also discussed VPC network egress impact and on-prem hot-warm routing.
action_items: Ava Martinez: share benchmark harness repo + README (due 2026-04-17)
Jonas Patel: run initial kv-batching microbench and send results (due 2026-04-20)
Leah Brooks: provide representative prompt set and 95th-percentile length distribution (due 2026-04-14)
Marcus Chen: open firewall rule/egress test window for on-prem lab (due 2026-04-16)
next_steps: Redwood to deliver microbench harness and sample configs
Customer to onboard prompt corpus to shared s3 and schedule bench window
Follow-up call to review numbers scheduled w/c 2026-04-27
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-10 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Jonas Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Redwood Solutions), Luis Romero (Redwood Benchmarks), Leah Brooks (Penumbra Head of ML), Marcus Chen (Penumbra Platform Eng), Rashid Alvi (Penumbra SRE), Priya Nair (Penumbra PM)

Summary/Context: Penumbra runs a streaming inference pipeline for document extraction + tool invocation on outputs. They're evaluating deterministic/JSON-mode for structured output with function calls, worried about latency spikes and throughput regression when enabling strict decoding and when models are quantized. They also operate hybrid infra (cloud VPC + on-prem inference pool) and want guidance on KV caching and batching tradeoffs.

[00:00] Ava: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, i'm ava from redwood. quick roll call?
[00:08] Leah: hey leah here, hi.
[00:10] Marcus: marcus here.
[00:12] Rashid: rashid, yep.
[00:15] Jonas: jonas on the se side.
[00:18] Maya: maya.
[00:20] Luis: luis.
[00:22] Priya: priya, thanks.

[00:30] Ava: great, objective for today is to get through the performance characteristics of deterministic output and function-chaining with your workload, surface any gotchas for kv cache and batching, and lay out a microbench plan. i'll hand to jonas to open with the problem outline.

[01:05] Jonas: thanks. so, quick thing — deterministic/json mode imposes token-level constraints to enforce a grammar and that can cause more decode steps and more rejections, uh and that leads to both CPU and small latency tails. we see this most when models are quantized and when kv cache isn't primed.

[01:40] Leah: can you say "primed" — like, if we warm with the same prefix are we good? our traffic is heavy on streaming docs, many short prefixes and then varying tail lengths.

[01:55] Jonas: yeah so priming helps. if you have high prefix reuse, kv cache hit rates go up and you recover the cost. but in deterministic mode there are extra checks (n-best rescoring, constrained filter passes) that each token might go through, so the marginal per-token cost is higher.

[02:30] Marcus: what's the ballpark — like percent hit on p95 or absolute ms? we need concrete so we can budget latency sla.

[02:42] Luis: from our benchmarks, enabling strict-json or parse-safe modes can add anywhere from 10-40% per-token latency depending on model & hardware. p50 is less affected, p95 shows bigger increases, particularly with quantized int8 kernels that have higher variance on some ops.

[03:10] Rashid: we use 0.25s p95 as our target for synchronous calls, so a 40% bump might push us over.

[03:20] Jonas: right, which is why we want to test with your prompt distributions. also batching plays a big role. for small single-request latency SLOs, smaller max batch size with microbatching helps, but that increases cost. there's a tradeoff.

[03:58] Priya: on the function-calling piece, are you seeing that the call orchestration (invoke tool) adds network hops that dominate the extra decode time? our orchestration is synchronous right now.

[04:10] Jonas: sometimes yes — especially if your tool/func host is external across VPC boundary. But we differentiate two sources: decode-side overhead (constrained decoding compute/time) and post-decode tool invocation latency (network + user service processing). We sometimes see the latter be bigger if the tool endpoint sits across a peered VPC or NAT.

[04:45] Leah: curious about kv cache behavior — if we do prefix caching across calls but then call a function that changes the conversation state, does the cache become less useful?

[04:56] Jonas: good question. cache keys are usually prefix+session, so if the function changes the context (e.g., inserts a long structured block), subsequent requests might have reduced reuse. But caching still helps for early tokens. Also our runtime supports partial cache invalidation — you can expire only recent segments.

[05:30] Ava: we should talk about quantization combos too — you may be running int8 to save cost; quantized kernels occasionally have slightly different distribution of op timings, some attention transpose kernels have jitter.

[05:50] Marcus: could you explain jitter vs steady slower throughput — i'm thinking our p95 spikes vs average.

[05:57] Jonas: jitter is variance per token — if a kernel takes variable time because of memory alignment or thread scheduling, you get spiky tails. Quantization can increase memory pressure or use alternate kernels with different perf curves.

[06:30] Luis: also worth noting: when deterministic mode rejects early tokens and forces n-best lookups, we may run additional forward passes or extra log-prob computations which show up in CPU time and latency.

[07:00] Leah: ok, for the function chain we have 2 calls: extract -> postprocess -> external classification. often the external classifier is hosted in our VPC. what are best practices to keep end-to-end latency predictable?

[07:18] Jonas: several: 1) colocate function hosts in same VPC / AZ or run them on Redwood Dedicated/Private to avoid NAT. 2) use an async pattern for non-blocking postprocess — respond to user while background job finishes, or 3) implement a tiny local verifier in the runtime to reduce full external roundtrips for most calls.

[07:45] Rashid: we prefer synchronous because of regulatory reasons — we need to serially validate outputs before ingest. can you support pinned dedicated on-prem to eliminate public egress?

[07:55] Ava: yes, Redwood Private on-prem is an option — it gives private control plane and you can run the runtime behind your internal network, that eliminates egress but introduces ops work, we can help with packaging.

[08:20] Marcus: returning to decode overhead — is there a knob to relax strictness when probability mass suggests a single valid parse? basically a heuristic to short-circuit expensive checks.

[08:35] Jonas: we have a "parse-confidence" threshold in beta: if top-k probability mass over constrained grammar is above X, we skip deeper n-best rescoring. it's not on by default in production yet but we can enable it for your pilot.

[09:00] Leah: that could save ms if your prompts are clean. We'll provide samples so you can tune threshold.

[09:12] Luis: note: when you enable parse-confidence skips, you should keep a fallback where if the top-k spells out an invalid json we re-run with stricter beams or route to a safer model; otherwise you risk corrupt structured outputs.

[09:45] Priya: about batching, what's the sweet spot? our traffic is bursty from ingestion pipelines.

[09:55] Jonas: for bursty streaming you might use two queues: low-latency fast-path (batch size <=4, strict single-request priority) and a throughput path (batch up to 32). Redwood runtime supports per-route autoscaling and queue priorities that can map to those.

[10:20] Marcus: does the KV cache interplay with batching? like, does a large batch reduce cache hit rate because different requests have different prefixes?

[10:32] Jonas: exactly. batching mixes sessions so cache locality drops. We do session-aware batching where we prioritize grouping requests with similar prefix hashes to improve shared KV reuse. That reduces per-token compute.

[11:00] Leah: perfect, please include that in the config doc.

[11:10] Ava: we'll do that. quick pause — any immediate architecture risks you see?

[11:20] Marcus: NATting between our on-prem and your hosted endpoints could add 30-80ms; we've seen that.

[11:28] Jonas: yep, network egress is often underestimated. For on-prem, plan to either run Private or set up high-throughput peering and allow dedicated subnets to eliminate double NAT.

[11:50] Leak (transcription glitch): "we also seen the quote of --"
[11:56] Leah: (laughs) yep.

[12:05] Luis: going to show a small chart — redwood's internal microbench across a medium LLM family: baseline unconstrained p95 210ms, strict-json on same quantized model p95 320ms; with kv cache primed p95 improves to 240ms. these are synthetic but directional.

[12:45] Jonas: two more things — function-call overhead can be amortized by batching tool invocations when you can. E.g., if you can aggregate multiple classification requests into a single RPC, that reduces network roundtrips. Also local caching of small tool responses helps.

[13:20] Priya: our tool responses are usually small. can we memoize by input hash?

[13:28] Jonas: yes memoization is a good strategy for idempotent deterministic tools; watch TTL for stateful ones.

[13:50] Leah: wanted to flag security — if we run KV cache across sessions or shared pools, what's the isolation model? we can't leak cached prefixes across customers.

[14:00] Ava: isolation is per-customer namespace by default. for Dedicated you get physical pools; for Hosted we enforce namespace isolation, and there are options for encrypted caches and KMS-wrapped keys.

[14:22] Marcus: ok. switching to the microbench plan — how do you propose we structure tests?

[14:30] Luis: propose matrix: models [base float16, int8-quant, q4_0], modes [unconstrained, strict-json, parse-confidence], cache [cold, warm], batching [1, 8, 32], tool-invoke [local, vpc-peered, external-nat]. run p50/p95/p99 and token-cost. We'll run for your prompt distribution.

[15:05] Leah: that sounds comprehensive. how long will that take?

[15:10] Luis: first pass for 10k examples ~24 hours of bench time; we can parallelize. produce initial report in 3 business days.

[15:25] Jonas: another nuance: when you do streaming responses with structured outputs, you might see mismatched partial parses — e.g., the model starts streaming text then we need a complete JSON object; streaming with constrained decode requires buffering until parse completion which adds latency to first complete object.

[15:50] Leah: so for streaming, are you recommending to avoid deterministic mode?

[15:57] Jonas: not necessarily. If you need immediate partial tokens, you can run a two-stream approach: a fast freeform stream for immediate UI, then a final strict pass to produce validated structured output. The UI shows streaming best-effort and then flips to final verified output.

[16:25] Priya: interesting. our clients want the validated JSON as soon as possible; sometimes we can accept slightly delayed final with a best-effort prefill.

[16:40] Marcus: on the on-prem note: we saw 12% better p95 when running in the same rack due to reduced jitter. So physical locality really matters for predictable tails.

[16:55] Jonas: yep. also scheduling and CPU neighbor noise on shared nodes can hurt quant kernels more — consider isolated cores or cgroups to pin critical threads.

[17:20] Ava: are there any concerns about model fallback logic and observability when deterministic mode fails? e.g., should we auto-fallback to a safer non-strict model?

[17:34] Jonas: yes. implement a fallback policy: retry with relaxed constraints and log a regression event; keep sample of failed prompts for offline eval. Redwood Console can surface those alerts and provide delta-quality metrics.

[17:55] Leah: good. Could Redwood also provide a small eval harness that flags false-negatives (when strict mode incorrectly rejects valid outputs)?

[18:05] Luis: absolutely — we can run your prompt set in parallel under both modes and produce a confusion matrix.

[18:25] Rashid: networking again — do you have any tips for reducing egress tail latency, aside from peering?

[18:32] Jonas: yes: 1) keep tool hosts in same AZ, 2) use private IP routing, 3) enable TCP keepalive and connection pooling so you avoid new TLS handshakes on every invoke, 4) if you must cross NAT, use UDP-based fast RPCs where possible or gRPC with long-lived connections.

[19:05] Priya: connection pooling seems low-hanging. we'll check our caller services.

[19:15] Ava: ok let's run through a concrete example from Leah — a 3-step chain where the model emits JSON which triggers two tool calls. walk me through what happens in runtime.

[19:30] Leah: sure. prompt -> model streams partial JSON -> runtime detects closing bracket -> constrained parse validated -> call tool A -> tool A returns, patch context -> model resumes -> emits final array -> call tool B.

[19:55] Jonas: pitfalls: partial streaming detection may mis-detect closing bracket in noisy outputs, you may re-run strict parse across the entire sequence which is more expensive; and if tool A is slow, the model is blocked waiting for the updated context. Consider optimistic continuation where you speculatively continue generation conditioned on probable tool responses, then reconcile after tool returns.

[20:30] Leah: speculative continuation sounds risky but could be worth it at 95th percentile.

[20:38] Luis: it's a tradeoff: speculative continuation adds complexity and potential rollbacks. For deterministic outputs though, it's often better to wait and keep correctness. We can quantify how often speculation would have been correct on your dataset.

[21:00] Marcus: can the runtime do partial speculative caching (store hypothetical KV state) to speed rollbacks?

[21:12] Jonas: yes, we have transactional-like KV patches in the runtime: speculative writes are isolated until commit. It increases memory but reduces recompute.

[21:35] Priya: talking about memory — with large parallel batches and kv caches, what's the memory footprint per-session? we have memory-constrained nodes.

[21:45] Luis: it varies by model and kv entries but plan for 200-600MB per active session depending on suffix lengths; with 1000 concurrent sessions you need careful sizing or a multi-tier cache (hot in memory, warm on nvme).

[22:10] Leah: do you support offloading KV to an external redis?

[22:15] Jonas: yes you can plug external kv stores but it adds network latency; better to use local memory-backed cache for hot tokens and an async warmer to fetch from external store.

[22:35] Rashid: for quantization: do you recommend any specific quant config for our use-case where correctness is important but cost matters?

[22:45] Jonas: q4_0 or int8 for cost balance; run your tests. q4 may produce slight quality deltas for rare tokens which might cause stricter decoders to reject; consider running strict mode on f16 for critical routes and quant for others.

[23:10] Priya: is dynamic quantization an option?

[23:15] Luis: dynamic quantization at runtime is tricky; we generally recommend static quantization profiles tuned per-model. Our Optimize team can recommend profiles per workload.

[23:40] Marcus: let's talk metrics — what should we collect during bench to diagnose decoding overheads precisely?

[23:50] Jonas: collect per-token CPU/GPU time, kernel-level metrics, KV cache hit/miss counts, number of n-best rescoring passes, bytes marshalled for function calls, network RTT to tool hosts, and end-to-end p50/p95/p99. Also store sample failure traces for debugging.

[24:20] Leah: can Redwood's console capture kernel metrics or do we need custom hooks?

[24:28] Luis: our runtime emits per-request traces that include kernel timings (best-effort), plus we can instrument further if you want deeper profiling with perf counters.

[24:50] Ava: taking notes — action item: we'll send bench harness and an example config.

[24:58] (audio: faint keyboard)

[25:10] Jonas: one more subtle item: when using constrained decoding with temperature or sampling-based settings disabled, you still might see fallback paths if tokenization ambiguities happen; tokenization differences across quantized kernels can cause unexpected token boundaries and produce parse errors. Keep tokenizer consistent across all runtime variants.

[25:45] Leah: we'll freeze tokenizer version in test config.

[26:00] Marcus: any recommended defaults for batch sizes for streaming endpoints?

[26:10] Jonas: start with max_batch 4 for low-latency route; throughput route 16-32. Also lower max latency target per batch to prevent long queuing.

[26:33] Luis: also set a per-session cap to avoid single requests blocking big batches; use priority lanes.

[26:50] Priya: do you have example autoscaling policies for mixed workloads?

[26:55] Ava: yes we'll attach sample autoscale yaml with thresholds for queue length, CPU utilization, and token backlog.

[27:10] Rashid: about observability — we need traces that tie token-level latency to specific kernels to show which layer causes p95 jumps.

[27:22] Jonas: we'll enable trace hooks that annotate per-token kernel calls in the console. sample visuals will be in the report.

[27:45] Leah: for the microbench, will you also include cost-per-token estimates?

[27:52] Luis: yes cost modeling included — raw compute cost + estimated network egress + amortized dedicated costs if using Dedicated.

[28:10] Priya: any legal/compliance issues if we run partial memos of customer prompts in Redwood benchmarks?

[28:18] Ava: we can sign an scp and redact prompts or run the bench inside Private so data never leaves your VPC. Options.

[28:35] Marcus: prefer private bench if possible. we'll provision a lab.

[28:42] Jonas: note: when benching in private, ensure you run the exact kernel builds we ship; sometimes enterprise builds differ slightly.

[29:00] Leah: what's the expected delta when moving from hosted to private? we care about parity.

[29:09] Luis: typically parity is good within 5-10% if hardware is comparable; differences mostly from network stack and kernel build flags on enterprise appliance.

[29:35] Ava: we're about halfway through. any deep technical questions?

[29:42] Priya: curious about the impact of TLS termination — if the runtime terminates TLS at the edge and then rpcs to internal, does that add jitter?

[29:52] Jonas: TLS termination offload is fine; jitter mainly comes from handshake frequency. reuse TLS sockets and enable session tickets to avoid negotiation per-call.

[30:10] (laptop sound)

[30:18] Luis: quick interruption — here's an example bench artifact: scenario A (q4_0, strict-json, kv warm, batch 8) p95 280ms; scenario B (f16, strict-json, kv warm, batch 8) p95 230ms. shows quant delta ~20%.

[30:45] Leah: helpful.

[30:50] Marcus: any gotchas for garbage collection in managed runtimes that could cause pauses?

[30:58] Jonas: yes, high-allocation Python tooling or some metrics collectors can cause safepoint pauses. Prefer low-GC runtimes or native hooks. Pin important threads.

[31:20] Priya: okay, last set — when strict-json fails, is the failure mode explicit so we can surface to end-user?

[31:30] Jonas: yes we return structured error codes and a failure payload that includes partial tokens and a rationale (e.g., tokenized invalid char at pos X).

[31:50] Leah: that will help for debugging.

[32:00] Ava: let's capture a concrete microbench run steps so you know what to prepare.

[32:10] Luis: Step 1: customer uploads 10k prompt corpus and labels for expected json shape. Step 2: Redwood runs matrix of configs per earlier table. Step 3: we produce p50/p95/p99, cost, failure cases, and quality diffs. Step 4: we meet to interpret results and recommend production config.

[32:40] Marcus: that's clear.

[32:45] Leah: small question: do you produce synthetic load that mimics arrival patterns? our production bursts are diurnal with micro-bursts.

[32:55] Luis: yes we can replay arrival patterns and also run Poisson burst models to simulate tail effects.

[33:10] Jonas: final note: for function chains, instrument correlation ids so you can trace token-to-tool calls easily in logs and the console.

[33:22] Priya: agreed. we'll add correlation id headers.

[33:30] (brief pause)

[33:40] Ava: ok action items recap: Ava sends harness, Jonas runs kv-batching microbench, Leah provides prompt corpus, Marcus opens lab egress window. Follow-up call week of April 27th. Anything else?

[33:58] Leah: please include recommended defaults for parse-confidence threshold.

[34:05] Jonas: will do.

[34:12] Rashid: please include network diagnostics checklist; i'll run it before bench.

[34:18] Ava: yes.

[34:30] (closing)

[34:35] Leah: thanks everyone.
[34:38] Marcus: thanks.
[34:40] Ava: thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[34:45] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: some proper nouns and product names may be slightly off (e.g., "parse-confidence" might appear as "parse confidence"; "Redwood Private" transcribed as "Redwood Private/Privy" in places). Occasional filler words and speaker attribution inconsistencies present.
